newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon seen selling Amana, moving plants.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon seen selling Amana, moving plants.

text.p: Raytheon Co is expected to shift some of its manufacturing facilities out of Massachusetts and sell its Amana appliance unit to help cut its debt from two proposed takeovers, analysts said.
Raytheon will shift missile production out of Massachusetts to lower cost facilities in Arizona, and could cut thousands of manufacturing, sales and administrative jobs, they said.
"Since they have duplicate facilities...they'll obviously go with the low-cost facility, which is not Massachusetts," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
Such a move, analysts said, would likely anger Massachusetts politicians, who granted Raytheon and other industrial companies a tax cut in return for a promise to keep jobs in the state.

Raytheon has hired consultants McKinsey & Co to examine how to cut costs and raise cash in order to pay its debt, which the company said will grow to $11 billion from $3.6 billion before the two proposed takeovers.
Bob McWade, a Raytheon spokesman, confirmed that the company hired McKinsey, but stressed that it will take three years to figure out how to cut costs associated with the mergers.
"Right now it's entirely too premature to speculate on what might happen over the next three years," he said.

Raytheon last month proposed buying Texas Instruments' defense assets for $3 billion in cash and paying $9.5 billion in cash and equity to General Motors Corp's for the aircraft unit of Hughes Electronics Corp.
The merger will create a defense giant, and Raytheon stressed the company would grow and needs to fill 2,500 jobs for engineers and technicians.
But the unnamed analyst said that Raytheon also plans to cut 8,500 jobs from overlapping areas.
"They talk somewhere in the order of a 10 percent reduction, which is somewhere around 8,500 positions," the analyst said.
He said Raytheon has downplayed talk of layoffs in order not to arouse political opposition to the mergers.
Gary Sparago, a corporate bond analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said he also expects plant closings and layoffs, but 8,500 job cuts may be too aggressive.

"I think there will be layoffs, although I don't think that's really a key part of the strategy," he said. "They were sort of downplaying the potential for head count reductions and that would make sense."
Sparago said the three companies compliment each other without excessive overlap.
Analysts said any layoffs are not expected to be announced until after well after the Hughes merger closes in the third quarter.
The high debt levels associated with the merger will force Raytheon to sell one of its commercial businesses, most likely Amana, analysts said.
"I would be very surprised if it's not sold by the end of the year," Sparago said.
Analysts estimate that Amana could fetch around $1 billion, he said. "Certainly it would go a long way to paying a lot of the debt they have assumed."
